Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Rioting has flared near Belfast on Saturday after the arrests of three men in the killings of two soldiers in Northern Ireland last week, police said. Two people in masks prepare to throw petrol bombs Saturday in Lurgan, Northern Ireland. Petrol bombs have been hurled at police in Lurgan, a town in County Armagh, 20 miles west of Belfast, police in Northern Ireland said. There are gangs of youths on the streets, authorities said, but there have been no arrests or injuries. Police announced the arrests on Saturday and said the three men have been taken to the police service's Serious Crime Suite in County Antrim. One of them, a dissident republican named Colin Duffy, is from Lurgan. They are the first arrests in connection with the March 7 shootings, which were the first fatal attack on British troops in the province for more than 12 years. The two British soldiers were shot dead at a base in Massereene, in Antrim, as they were preparing to ship out for duty in Afghanistan. The soldiers, Cengiz "Pat" Azimkar, 21, and Mark Quinsey, 23, had already packed their bags and changed into desert uniforms, authorities said. Two masked gunmen with automatic rifles shot them as the soldiers picked up a pizza delivery at the barracks, authorities said. Two other soldiers and the two pizza delivery men were seriously wounded. The shooting has sparked fears of a return to the sectarian violence that Northern Ireland suffered until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, a period known as The Troubles. A militant splinter group, the Real IRA, reportedly claimed it had carried out the attack on the soldiers. Two days after the soldiers were killed, a police officer was killed in a shooting southwest of Belfast. Constable Stephen Carroll was one of four officers who were responding to call in Craigavon when his vehicle came under fire and he was killed. Three people have been arrested in connection with the police officer's death. The Continuity IRA, a republican splinter group that does not accept the Good Friday Agreement, said it had killed Carroll, Britain's Press Association reported. Politicians from across the political spectrum have condemned the killings, with Sinn Fein deputy leader Martin McGuinness calling the killers "traitors to the island of Ireland." Sinn Fein is a predominantly Catholic party that wants Northern Ireland to leave the United Kingdom and become part of the Republic of Ireland. The party is widely thought to be linked to the Irish Republican Army. Danny Kennedy, deputy leader of the loyalist Ulster Unionist Party, which wants Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom, also condemned the attack as "wicked and murderous."

**Renewed fears of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland after attacks on troops and police**

**Belfast, Northern Ireland** — A series of deadly attacks on British security forces has stirred fears that dissident republican groups are trying to drag Northern Ireland back toward the sectarian violence that scarred the region for decades.

The concerns intensified after two British soldiers were shot dead outside Massereene Barracks in Antrim, northwest of Belfast, in an attack claimed by the Real IRA, a breakaway republican faction opposed to the peace process. Days later, a police officer was killed in Craigavon, County Armagh, in an attack claimed by the Continuity IRA, another dissident group.

The killings marked the first deaths of British soldiers in Northern Ireland in more than a decade and the first fatal attack on a police officer there in years, jolting a society that has made substantial progress since the 1998 Good Friday Agreement largely ended the conflict known as **The Troubles**.

For nearly 30 years, Northern Ireland was gripped by violence between mainly Catholic republicans, who wanted to end British rule and unite with the Republic of Ireland, and mainly Protestant unionists, who wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom. British troops, police, loyalist paramilitaries and republican groups were all part of a conflict that left more than 3,500 people dead.

The peace accord created a power-sharing government between unionists and nationalists and led to the disarmament of the Irish Republican Army. But small dissident groups rejected the settlement, arguing that armed struggle should continue.

Sinn Fein, the political party historically linked to the republican movement and now a central player in Northern Ireland’s government, strongly condemned the latest attacks. Party leaders said those responsible had no mandate and were attempting to undermine the peace process.

Martin McGuinness, a senior Sinn Fein figure and former IRA commander who became deputy first minister, described the attackers as enemies of the people of Ireland and said they would not succeed in pushing Northern Ireland back into conflict. Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams also urged communities to cooperate with police investigations, a significant position for a party that once opposed the legitimacy of Northern Ireland’s police service.

Unionist politicians also denounced the violence and called for a unified response. Democratic Unionist Party leaders said the killings were an attack not only on security forces but on the political institutions created by the peace agreement. Unionists urged all parties, including Sinn Fein, to demonstrate unequivocal support for the police and the rule of law.

Officials on both sides said the attacks appeared designed to provoke retaliation and inflame old sectarian divisions. So far, political leaders have presented a united front, warning that dissident militants remain small in number but dangerous.

Security has been tightened in several areas, and police have appealed for information from the public. Community leaders say the coming days will be a test of whether Northern Ireland’s peace is strong enough to withstand efforts by armed groups to destabilize it.

For many residents, the fear is not that the region will immediately return to the worst days of The Troubles, but that even a handful of attacks could reopen wounds that have never fully healed.

## Colin Duffy and Two Others Arrested After Massereene Killings as Dissident Republican Tensions Flare

Northern Ireland faced renewed security tensions in March 2009 after police arrested prominent republican Colin Duffy and two other men in connection with the murders of British soldiers Cengiz “Pat” Azimkar and Mark Quinsey outside Massereene Barracks in Antrim.

Azimkar, 21, from London, and Quinsey, 23, from Birmingham, were shot dead on 7 March 2009 as they collected pizzas at the gates of the barracks. Several other people, including soldiers and civilian delivery workers, were wounded in the attack. The soldiers were due to deploy to Afghanistan shortly afterward.

The killings were claimed by the Real IRA, a dissident republican group opposed to the Northern Ireland peace process and the Good Friday Agreement. The attack was widely condemned across the political spectrum, including by Sinn Féin leaders, unionist parties, the Irish and British governments, and community representatives.

Police later arrested Colin Duffy, a well-known republican from Lurgan, along with two other men, as part of the investigation into the Massereene shootings. Duffy had long been associated in public reporting with dissident republican circles, though he denied involvement in the murders. The arrests triggered unrest in parts of County Armagh and near Belfast, where youths clashed with police, threw petrol bombs, and blocked roads. The disturbances were seen as a sign of heightened tensions following the security operation and the broader dissident republican campaign.

The Massereene attack was followed two days later by the killing of Police Service of Northern Ireland officer Stephen Carroll in Craigavon, County Armagh. That murder was claimed by the Continuity IRA, another dissident republican organization. Carroll was the first police officer killed in Northern Ireland since the formation of the PSNI, making the attack particularly significant and raising fears that dissident groups were attempting to destabilize the peace settlement.

Despite the shock caused by the killings, political leaders urged calm and insisted that Northern Ireland would not return to the violence of the Troubles. The attacks prompted an intensified police response against dissident republicans and renewed public debate about the threat posed by small armed groups rejecting the peace process.

Colin Duffy was later charged in connection with the Massereene attack but was acquitted in 2012 after a high-profile trial. The case remained one of the most significant dissident republican prosecutions of the post-Good Friday Agreement era.
